modern_osis:
Original heading

David's struggle with, and triumph over a strong temptation to distrust God, and betake himself to indirect means for his own safety, in a time of danger.

Trusting the Lord rather than worldly advice

Everyone who sincerely fears and serves God may trust him with confidence.

Before David described his temptation to distrust the Lord, he stated his decision to trust him in life and in death.

Believers may not be frightened by their enemies, yet they can still be tempted by the fears of their friends.

Well-meaning companions may persuade them to abandon their position or neglect their assigned work.

These friends see the danger but fail to recognize the believer's safety in God.

Their advice comes from worldly calculation rather than heavenly wisdom.

The truths of faith are the foundation of Christian confidence and hope.

We must hold firmly to them against every temptation to unbelief.

Without God to turn to, God to trust and the hope of eternal happiness, believers would be ruined.

The prosperity of wicked people and the hardship endured by godly people had tested David's faith.

Yet we do not need to climb to heaven to bring down a God we can trust.

His word is close to us, and God is present in his word.

His Spirit dwells within his saints, who are living temples.

The Lord is that Spirit.

God governs the world.

We may know only how people appear.

God knows what they truly are, as a refiner knows gold after testing it.

He examines hearts with eyes that cannot be deceived.

When the Lord afflicts righteous people, he tests them for their ultimate good.

Persecutors and oppressors may prosper temporarily, but if they remain unrepentant they will perish.

God is holy and therefore hates evil.

He is a righteous Judge and therefore will punish it.

At death, the wicked are carried away in a dreadful storm.

Every person receives an appointed portion.

Sinner, consider your danger: judgment is approaching, and without repentance death leads toward eternal wrath.

Hurry to the cross of Christ.

Ask yourself: what is the relationship between God and my soul?

Is Christ my hope, my comfort and my protection?

Only through him can the soul safely pass through all its troubles and spiritual conflicts.
classic_reading:
[Ps.11.1]
Chapter 11
David's struggle with, and triumph over a strong temptation to distrust God, and betake himself to indirect means for his own safety, in a time of danger.
--Those that truly fear God and serve him, are welcome to put their trust in him. The psalmist, before he gives an account of his temptation to distrust God, records his resolution to trust in Him, as that by which he was resolved to live and die. The believer, though not terrified by his enemies, may be tempted, by the fears of his friends, to desert his post, or neglect his work. They perceive his danger, but not his security; they give him counsel that savours of worldly policy, rather than of heavenly wisdom. The principles of religion are the foundations on which the faith and hope of the righteous are built. We are concerned to hold these fast against all temptations to unbelief; for believers would be undone, if they had not God to go to, God to trust in, and future bliss to hope for. The prosperity of wicked people in their wicked, evil ways, and the straits and distresses which the best men are sometimes brought into, tried David's faith. We need not say, Who shall go up to heaven, to fetch us thence a God to trust in? The word is nigh us, and God in the word; his Spirit is in his saints, those living temples, and the Lord is that Spirit. This God governs the world. We may know what men seem to be, but God knows what they are, as the refiner knows the value of gold when he has tried it. God is said to try with his eyes, because he cannot err, or be imposed upon. If he afflicts good people, it is for their trial, therefore for their good. However persecutors and oppressors may prosper awhile, they will for ever perish. God is a holy God, and therefore hates them. He is a righteous Judge, and will therefore punish them. In what a horrible tempest are the wicked hurried away at death! Every man has the portion of his cup assigned him. Impenitent sinner, mark your doom! The last call to repentance is about to be addressed to you, judgement is at hand; through the gloomy shade of death you pass into the region of eternal wrath. Hasten then, O sinner, to the cross of Christ. How stands the case between God and our souls? Is Christ our hope, our consolation, our security? Then, not otherwise, will the soul be carried through all its difficulties and conflicts.

modern_osis:
Original heading

The psalmist begs help of God, because there were none among men whom he durst trust.

Seeking God amid moral decline

This Psalm provides wise thoughts and prayers for difficult times.

What makes a time truly bad?

Ask worldly-minded people, and they will mention lack of money, declining trade or the destruction caused by war.

But Scripture points to deeper causes.

Perilous times arrive when sin becomes widespread (2 Timothy 3:1).

When godliness declines, the times are genuinely evil.

The One who made the human mouth will judge how it is used—whether for proud, profane, deceitful or even useless words.

When poor and needy people are oppressed, times are very bad.

God hears their sighs and sees their suffering.

When wickedness becomes widespread and those holding authority encourage it, the situation is especially grave.

Yet God provides three consolations for such times.

First, we can approach the Lord to ask him to put right every wrong.

Second, he will punish and restrain those who persist in pride and falsehood.

Third, he will deliver his oppressed people in the most suitable time.

Human beings may lie, but God remains faithful.

People may fail our trust, but God can be trusted.

His word is as precious and reliable as silver refined repeatedly to the highest purity.

Its truth and power have been demonstrated again and again.

However dark the age becomes, God will preserve his chosen remnant.

Until the end of the world, there will continue to be proud and wicked generations.

But God's people have been entrusted to Jesus Christ our Savior.

No one can snatch them from his hands.

They are built upon Christ the Rock, safe even against the fiercest persecution and temptation.
classic_reading:
[Ps.12.1]
Chapter 12
The psalmist begs help of God, because there were none among men whom he durst trust.
--This psalm furnishes good thoughts for bad times; a man may comfort himself with such meditations and prayers. Let us see what makes the times bad, and when they may be said to be so. Ask the children of this world, What makes the times bad? they will tell you, Scarcity of money, decay of trade, and the desolations of war, make the times bad: but the Scripture lays the badness of the times on causes of another nature, [2Tim.3.1] 2Ti 3:1, &c.: perilous times shall come, for sin shall abound; and of this David complains. When piety decays times really are bad. He who made man's mouth will call him to an account for his proud, profane, dissembling, or even useless words. When the poor and needy are oppressed, then the times are very bad. God himself takes notice of the oppression of the poor, and the sighing of the needy. When wickedness abounds, and is countenanced by those in authority, then the times are very bad. See with what good things we are here furnished for such bad times; and we cannot tell what times we may be reserved for. 1. We have a God to go to, from whom we may ask and expect the redress of all our grievances. 2. God will certainly punish and restrain false and proud men. 3. God will work deliverance for his oppressed people. His help is given in the fittest time. Though men are false, God is faithful; though they are not to be trusted, God is. The preciousness of God's word is compared to silver refined to the highest degree. How many proofs have been given of its power and truth! God will secure his chosen remnant, however bad the times are. As long as the world stands, there will be a generation of proud and wicked men. But all God's people are put into the hands of Christ our Saviour; there they are in safety, for none can pluck them thence; being built on Him, the Rock, they are safe, notwithstanding temptation or persecution come with ever so much force upon them.

modern_osis:
Original heading

The psalmist complains that God had long withdrawn. He earnestly prays for comfort. He assures himself of an answer of peace.

From long sorrow to confidence in mercy

At times God hides his face, and his children are left uncertain about their relationship with him.

They feel this more deeply than any outward hardship.

Yet believers often burden themselves with anxieties beyond what is necessary.

The bread of sorrow may become their daily food.

Our own Master, Jesus Christ, was a Man of Sorrows.

During long afflictions, a common temptation is to imagine that suffering will never end.

People who have been without joy for a long time may begin losing hope as well.

Let our complaints drive us to prayer, not away from it.

Nothing is more devastating to the soul than feeling deprived of God's favor.

Nothing is more reviving than the return of that favor.

The sudden, joyful changes recorded in the Psalms are remarkable.

In verse 4, everything seems full of gloomy despair.

But in verse 5, the psalmist rises above his fears and throws himself entirely upon the mercy and care of his divine Redeemer.

See the power of faith and the goodness of approaching God.

When we bring our troubles to the throne of grace and leave them there, we can depart as Hannah did, no longer looking sad (1 Samuel 1:18).

The psalmist's faith rested upon God's mercy, not upon any merit of his own.

Once he trusted that mercy, his heart rejoiced in salvation.

Joy and peace come through believing.

He became so confident of God's promised salvation that he spoke as though it were already accomplished.

Believers may pray in the same way, abandoning every hope except God's mercy through the Savior's blood.

Sometimes their burdens lift suddenly.

At other times relief comes slowly.

When comfort returns, they recognize that many earlier fears were unnecessary and confess that the Lord has dealt generously with them.
classic_reading:
[Ps.13.1]
Chapter 13
The psalmist complains that God had long withdrawn. He earnestly prays for comfort. He assures himself of an answer of peace.
--God sometimes hides his face, and leaves his own children in the dark concerning their interest in him: and this they lay to heart more than any outward trouble whatever. But anxious cares are heavy burdens with which believers often load themselves more than they need. The bread of sorrows is sometimes the saint's daily bread; our Master himself was a man of sorrows. It is a common temptation, when trouble lasts long, to think that it will last always. Those who have long been without joy, begin to be without hope. We should never allow ourselves to make any complaints but what drive us to our knees. Nothing is more killing to a soul than the want of God's favour; nothing more reviving than the return of it. The sudden, delightful changes in the book of Psalms, are often very remarkable. We pass from depth of despondency to the height of religious confidence and joy. It is thus, ver. 5. All is gloomy dejection in ver. 4; but here the mind of the despondent worshipper rises above all its distressing fears, and throws itself, without reserve, on the mercy and care of its Divine Redeemer. See the power of faith, and how good it is to draw near to God. If we bring our cares and griefs to the throne of grace, and leave them there, we may go away like Hannah, and our countenances will be no more said, [1Sam.1.18] 1Sa 1:18. God's mercy is the support of the psalmist's faith. Finding I have that to trust to, I am comforted, though I have no merit of my own. His faith in God's mercy filled his heart with joy in his salvation; for joy and peace come by believing. He has dealt bountifully with me. By faith he was as confident of salvation, as if it had been completed already. In this way believers pour out their prayers, renouncing all hopes but in the mercy of God through the Saviour's blood: and sometimes suddenly, at others gradually, they will find their burdens removed, and their comforts restored; they then allow that their fears and complaints were unnecessary, and acknowledge that the Lord hath dealt bountifully with them.

modern_osis:
Original heading

A description of the depravity of human nature, and the deplorable corruption of a great part of mankind.

Sin, human corruption and salvation from Zion

The fool says within the heart, “There is no God.”

The sinner described rejects the existence of a Judge governing the world and a Providence ruling human affairs.

But the denial begins within the heart.

Such a person cannot truly establish that God does not exist.

Instead, the person wishes there were no God and takes pleasure in the mere possibility that no divine judgment will come.

This is foolishness.

The sinner's wicked and irreverent conduct is both evidence of that folly and a cause of it.

God's word reveals the thoughts and desires behind it.

No one willingly denies divine accountability in this way until sin has hardened the heart so deeply that having no Judge appears desirable.

The disease of sin has infected all humanity.

Everyone has turned aside.

No one does good as the holy law demands—not even one.

Whatever good exists in human beings or is done through them comes from God's work within them, not from their own independent goodness.

People have turned away from the path of obedience and happiness and entered paths leading to ruin.

We should grieve over human corruption and recognize how greatly we need God's grace.

It is therefore no surprise that Scripture insists we must be born again.

We should not rest in anything less than union with Christ and a new creation through his Holy Spirit, producing holiness.

The psalmist tried to warn sinners who imagined themselves wise, upright and secure.

Those who show no concern for God's poor and his people show that they do not truly love God.

People continue committing wrong because they do not seek God's grace through prayer.

How much good can we expect from a life without prayer?

People unwilling to fear God may nevertheless become terrified by something as small as a shaking leaf.

The knowledge of our common corruption should make salvation coming from Zion precious to us.

In heaven alone will all the redeemed rejoice completely and forever.

The world is deeply sinful—how we should long for the Messiah to come and transform it!

The victories of Zion's King will be the joy of Zion's children.

Christ's second coming will finally overthrow the rule of sin and Satan and complete salvation.

This hope should comfort God's people amid the sins committed by sinners and the suffering endured by saints.
classic_reading:
[Ps.14.1]
Chapter 14
A description of the depravity of human nature, and the deplorable corruption of a great part of mankind.
--The fool hath said in his heart, There is no God. The sinner here described is an atheist, one that saith there is no Judge or Governor of the world, no Providence ruling over the affairs of men. He says this in his heart. He cannot satisfy himself that there is none, but wishes there were none, and pleases himself that it is possible there may be none; he is willing to think there is none. This sinner is a fool; he is simple and unwise, and this is evidence of it: he is wicked and profane, and this is the cause. The word of God is a discerner of these thoughts. No man will say, There is no God, till he is so hardened in sin, that it is become his interest that there should be none to call him to an account. The disease of sin has infected the whole race of mankind. They are all gone aside, there is none that doeth good, no, not one. Whatever good is in any of the children of men, or is done by them, it is not of themselves, it is God's work in them. They are gone aside from the right way of their duty, the way that leads to happiness, and are turned into the paths of the destroyer. Let us lament the corruption of our nature, and see what need we have of the grace of God: let us not marvel that we are told we must be born again. And we must not rest in any thing short of union with Christ, and a new creation to holiness by his Spirit. The psalmist endeavours to convince sinners of the evil and danger of their way, while they think themselves very wise, and good, and safe. Their wickedness is described. Those that care not for God's people, for God's poor, care not for God himself. People run into all manner of wickedness, because they do not call upon God for his grace. What good can be expected from those that live without prayer? But those that will not fear God, may be made to fear at the shaking of a leaf. All our knowledge of the depravity of human nature should endear to us salvation out of Zion. But in heaven alone shall the whole company of the redeemed rejoice fully, and for evermore. The world is bad; oh that the Messiah would come and change its character! There is universal corruption; oh for the times of reformation! The triumphs of Zion's King will be the joys of Zion's children. The second coming of Christ, finally to do away the dominion of sin and Satan, will be the completing of this salvation, which is the hope, and will be the joy of every Israelite indeed. With this assurance we should comfort ourselves and one another, under the sins of sinners and sufferings of saints.

modern_osis:
Original heading

The way to heaven, if we would be happy, we must be holy. We are encouraged to walk in that way.

The character of a citizen of Zion

This Psalm asks who belongs among the citizens of Zion.

The glorified saints are happy because they dwell on God's holy mountain.

They are at home there and will remain there forever.

We should examine whether we have a place among them.

The Psalm gives a clear and practical answer.

Scripture faithfully directs anyone sincerely wanting to know the path of duty, and conscience helps apply that direction.

A citizen of Zion is sincere in faith.

Such a person is genuinely what they claim to be and seeks to obey all God's will.

They deal justly with God and other people, speaking the truth from the heart.

They reject deceit, fraud and dishonest gain.

No bargain obtained through lies can truly be a good or profitable one.

Anyone who cheats a neighbor will eventually discover that the greatest injury fell upon the cheater.

The faithful person is careful not to harm anyone.

Such people do not slander others or turn their faults into daily entertainment.

They interpret others' conduct charitably.

When a malicious story is told, they try to correct it.

If they cannot, they do not pass it on.

They evaluate people according to character and true godliness rather than wealth or public reputation.

They do not despise a person's faith because that person is poor or occupies a humble position.

They recognize that sincere godliness confers more honor than wealth or a famous name.

They seek fellowship with godly people, appreciate their prayers and gladly show them kindness and respect.

By these marks we can examine ourselves.

A good and wise person may make a promise that later proves costly.

But a promise must still be kept even if this requires personal or family sacrifice.

It is better to bear loss than to wrong a neighbor.

God's people refuse to gain wealth through extortion or bribery.

No hope of personal advantage should persuade them to injure a righteous cause.

Every genuinely living member of Christ's church, like the church as a whole, is built upon a Rock.

The person who lives this way will not ultimately be shaken.

God's grace will remain sufficient.

But such attitudes and conduct can arise together only through repentance from sin, faith in the Savior and love for him.

Let us examine and test ourselves accordingly.
classic_reading:
[Ps.15.1]
Chapter 15
The way to heaven, if we would be happy, we must be holy. We are encouraged to walk in that way.
--Here is a very serious question concerning the character of a citizen of Zion. It is the happiness of glorified saints, that they dwell in the holy hill; they are at home there, they shall be for ever there. It concerns us to make it sure to ourselves that we have a place among them. A very plain and particular answer is here given. Those who desire to know their duty, will find the Scripture a very faithful director, and conscience a faithful monitor. A citizen of Zion is sincere in his religion. He is really what he professes to be, and endeavours to stand complete in all the will of God. He is just both to God and man; and, in speaking to both, speaks the truth in his heart. He scorns and abhors wrong and fraud; he cannot reckon that a good bargain, nor a saving one, which is made with a lie; and knows that he who wrongs his neighbour will prove, in the end, to have most injured himself. He is very careful to do hurt to no man. He speaks evil of no man, makes not others' faults the matter of his common talk; he makes the best of every body, and the worst of nobody. If an ill-natured story be told him, he will disprove it if he can; if not, it goes no further. He values men by their virtue and piety. Wicked people are vile people, worthless, and good for nothing; so the word signifies. He thinks the worse of no man's piety for his poverty and mean condition. He reckons that serious piety puts honour upon a man, more than wealth, or a great name. He honours such, desires their conversation and an interest in their prayers, is glad to show them respect, or do them a kindness. By this we may judge of ourselves in some measure. Even wise and good men may swear to their own hurt: but see how strong the obligation is, a man must rather suffer loss to himself and his family, than wrong his neighbour. He will not increase his estate by extortion, or by bribery. He will not, for any gain, or hope of it to himself, do any thing to hurt a righteous cause. Every true living member of the church, like the church itself, is built upon a Rock. He that doeth these things shall not be moved for ever. The grace of God shall always be sufficient for him. The union of these tempers and this conduct, can only spring from repentance for sin, faith in the Saviour, and love to him. In these respects let us examine and prove our own selves.

modern_osis:
Original heading

This psalm begins with expressions of devotion, which may be applied to Christ; but ends with such confidence of a resurrection, as must be applied to Christ, and to him only.

David's devotion and the hope of Christ's resurrection

David sought God's protection with joyful confidence.

Everyone who has acknowledged the Lord as their own Lord should remember that commitment often, draw comfort from it and live consistently with it.

David gave himself to honoring God by serving God's people.

We must become saints on earth if we hope to join the saints in heaven.

Those renewed by divine grace and devoted to God's glory are saints already.

God's people in this world are excellent, though some are so poor that they need practical kindness.

David resolved not to share in works of spiritual darkness.

He renewed his deliberate choice of God as his portion and happiness, took comfort from it and gave God the glory.

Most people choose this world as their greatest good.

But the faithful person says: However poor my circumstances may be, let me enjoy God's love and favor, be accepted by him and have the promised right to future life and happiness. That is enough.

Heaven is our true inheritance, home, rest and everlasting good.

We should consider the present world merely the country through which we travel toward our Father's house.

Anyone who has God as the appointed portion possesses a beautiful inheritance.

Return to rest, my soul.

People ruled by grace continue desiring more of God, but not more than God.

They are satisfied with his loving kindness and do not envy others' merely physical pleasures.

Yet without his sustaining grace we are foolish enough to surrender real mercies for empty substitutes.

God had counseled David through his word and Spirit.

As he meditated during the night, his own thoughts reinforced the determination to live by faith for God.

The apostle Peter quoted verses 8–11 in his Pentecost sermon (Acts 2:25–31).

Peter declared that David spoke of Jesus Christ, especially his resurrection.

As Christ is the Head of his body, the church, these verses also encourage believers who are guided and strengthened by Christ's Spirit.

Always place the Lord before you.

Then your heart and tongue may rejoice in him.

Death destroys ordinary earthly hopes, but not the hope of a true Christian.

Christ's resurrection is the pledge of the believer's own resurrection.

Sorrow belongs to the present world.

In heaven there is fullness of joy, and where earthly pleasures quickly vanish, the pleasures at God's right hand endure forever.

Lord, through your beloved Son and our Savior, show us the path of life.

Justify our souls now, and raise our bodies on the last day, when earthly sorrow becomes heavenly joy and pain becomes everlasting happiness.
classic_reading:
[Ps.16.1]
Chapter 16
This psalm begins with expressions of devotion, which may be applied to Christ; but ends with such confidence of a resurrection, as must be applied to Christ, and to him only.
--David flees to God's protection, with cheerful, believing confidence. Those who have avowed that the Lord is their Lord, should often put themselves in mind of what they have done, take the comfort of it, and live up to it. He devotes himself to the honour of God, in the service of the saints. Saints on earth we must be, or we shall never be saints in heaven. Those renewed by the grace of God, and devoted to the glory of God, are saints on earth. The saints in the earth are excellent ones, yet some of them so poor, that they needed to have David's goodness extended to them. David declares his resolution to have no fellowship with the works of darkness; he repeats the solemn choice he had made of God for his portion and happiness, takes to himself the comfort of the choice, and gives God the glory of it. This is the language of a devout and pious soul. Most take the world for their chief good, and place their happiness in the enjoyments of it; but how poor soever my condition is in this world, let me have the love and favour of God, and be accepted of him; let me have a title by promise to life and happiness in the future state; and I have enough. Heaven is an inheritance; we must take that for our home, our rest, our everlasting good, and look upon this world to be no more ours, than the country through which is our road to our Father's house. Those that have God for their portion, have a goodly heritage. Return unto thy rest, O my soul, and look no further. Gracious persons, though they still covet more of God, never covet more than God; but, being satisfied of his loving-kindness, are abundantly satisfied with it: they envy not any their carnal mirth and delights. But so ignorant and foolish are we, that if left to ourselves, we shall forsake our own mercies for lying vanities. God having given David counsel by his word and Spirit, his own thoughts taught him in the night season, and engaged him by faith to live to God. Verses #(8-11), are quoted by St. Peter in his first sermon, after the pouring out of the Spirit on the day of Pentecost, [Acts.2.25-Acts.2.31] Ac 2:25-31; he declared that David in them speaks concerning Christ, and particularly of his resurrection. And Christ being the Head of the body, the church, these verses may be applied to all Christians, guided and animated by the Spirit of Christ; and we may hence learn, that it is our wisdom and duty to set the Lord always before us. And if our eyes are ever toward God, our hearts and tongues may ever rejoice in him. Death destroys the hope of man, but not the hope of a real Christian. Christ's resurrection is an earnest of the believer's resurrection. In this world sorrow is our lot, but in heaven there is joy, a fulness of joy; our pleasures here are for a moment, but those at God's right hand are pleasures for evermore. Through this thy beloved Son, and our dear Saviour, thou wilt show us, O Lord, the path of life; thou wilt justify our souls now, and raise our bodies by thy power at the last day; when earthly sorrow shall end in heavenly joy, pain in everlasting happiness.

Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesDavid's integrity.1–7The character of his enemies. His hope of happiness.8–15
David prays with an upright heart (verses 1–7)

This Psalm is a prayer.

Prayers that only pretend to be sincere are useless.

But when our hearts lead our prayers, God receives them graciously.

David was accustomed to prayer.

He had not waited until suffering and danger to begin seeking God.

His faith therefore encouraged him to expect a hearing.

Steadfast determination and vigilance against sins of speech provide important evidence of integrity.

Knowing the natural human inclination toward evil and his own particular temptations, David had used God's word as protection against Satan's destructive paths.

It brings comfort in trouble to remember that grace has enabled us to avoid sinful ways.

Those following God's paths should pray continually that he will keep their feet steady on those paths.

David asked God to hold him up.

Everyone who wants to continue in divine service must obtain fresh daily strength and grace through faith and prayer.

He requested the Lord's wonderful loving kindness—not merely ordinary gifts but the special favor God shows to those who love his name.

Protection amid hostile enemies and eternal hope (verses 8–15)

David was surrounded by enemies and asked the Lord to keep him safe.

Henry understands the prayer as pointing prophetically toward Jesus Christ, preserved through every trial of humiliation until the glory and joy of exaltation.

It also teaches Christians to entrust their souls to God, believing he will preserve them for his heavenly kingdom.

Our worst enemies are those who threaten our souls.

Those who threaten our bodies act under divine Providence.

They are like God's sword, which cannot move without his permission and which he will put away when its work is finished.

They are like his hand, by which he disciplines his people.

We cannot escape God's hand except by fleeing into it.

It brings comfort when human power seems terrifying to remember that every such power depends upon God's sovereignty.

Most people consider worldly possessions their highest good and make no provision for the coming life.

What this world calls treasures becomes worthless rubbish when compared with eternal blessings.

The poorest and most afflicted Christian need not envy someone who possesses the world but has no better portion.

Clothed in Christ's righteousness, with a heart and life renewed by grace, may we look upon God's face by faith and continually set him before us.

Each morning may his likeness, shown in Scripture and impressed upon us by renewing grace, satisfy our hearts.

True eternal happiness is prepared for those who are justified and sanctified.

They receive it when the soul awakens at death from its bodily life, and when the body rises at the resurrection from the grave.

No soul is fully satisfied except in God's favor and gracious work.

Even that satisfaction will not become complete until heaven.
classic_reading:
[Ps.17.1-Ps.17.7]
Chapter 17
Chapter Outline
David's integrity. | (1-7) |
The character of his enemies. His hope of happiness. | (8-15) |
Verses 1-7
This psalm is a prayer. Feigned prayers are fruitless; but if our hearts lead our prayers, God will meet them with his favour. The psalmist had been used to pray, so that it was not his distress and danger that now first brought him to his duty. And he was encouraged by his faith to expect God would notice his prayers. Constant resolution and watchfulness against sins of the tongue, will be a good evidence of our integrity. Aware of man's propensity to wicked works, and of his own peculiar temptations, David had made God's word his preservative from the paths of Satan, which lead to destruction. If we carefully avoid the paths of sin, it will be very lead to destruction. If we carefully avoid the paths of sin, it will be very comfortable in the reflection, when we are in trouble. Those that are, through grace, going in God's paths, should pray that their goings may be held up in those paths. David prays, Lord, still hold me up. Those who would proceed and persevere in the ways of God, must, by faith prayer, get daily fresh supplies of grace and strength from him. Show thy marvellous loving-kindness, distinguishing favours, not common mercies, but be gracious to me; do as thou usest to do to those who love thy name.
[Ps.17.8-Ps.17.15]
Verses 8-15
Being compassed with enemies, David prays to God to keep him in safety. This prayer is a prediction that Christ would be preserved, through all the hardships and difficulties of his humiliation, to the glories and joys of his exalted state, and is a pattern to Christians to commit the keeping of their souls to God, trusting him to preserve them to his heavenly kingdom. Those are our worst enemies, that are enemies to our souls. They are God's sword, which cannot move without him, and which he will sheathe when he has done his work with it. They are his hand, by which he chastises his people. There is no fleeing from God's hand, but by fleeing to it. It is very comfortable, when we are in fear of the power of man, to see it dependent upon, and in subjection to the power of God. Most men look on the things of this world as the best things; and they look no further, nor show any care to provide for another life. The things of this world are called treasures, they are so accounted; but to the soul, and when compared with eternal blessings, they are trash. The most afflicted Christian need not envy the most prosperous men of the world, who have their portion in this life. Clothed with Christ's righteousness, having through his grace a good heart and a good life, may we by faith behold God's face, and set him always before us. When we awake every morning, may we be satisfied with his likeness set before us in his word, and with his likeness stamped upon us by his renewing grace. Happiness in the other world is prepared only for those that are justified and sanctified: they shall be put in possession of it when the soul awakes, at death, out of its slumber in the body, and when the body awakes, at the resurrection, out of its slumber in the grave. There is no satisfaction for a soul but in God, and in his good will towards us, and his good work in us; yet that satisfaction will not be perfect till we come to heaven.

The opening words, “I will love you, Lord, my strength,” express the main message of the Psalm.

Those who truly love God can rejoice in him as their Rock and Refuge and confidently call upon him.

When God grants deliverance, we should consider all the details that reveal his power and kindness.

David prayed, and God proved himself a God who hears prayer.

When we pray as David did, we may trust the same gracious God.

The description of God's majestic appearing, especially in verses 7–15, goes beyond what happened in the ordinary history of Jesse's son.

God will not merely bring his people out of trouble at the proper time.

He will also support them under it while it lasts.

The eighteenth verse directs Henry's thoughts to Gethsemane and Calvary.

Christ faced his deepest distress when Judas betrayed him, his friends abandoned him, the crowd mocked him, the comfort of his Father's love was withheld and the powers of darkness assailed him.

Even when we recognize many personal missteps, we must avoid a deliberate and settled departure from him.

David kept God's commands before his eyes.

Our careful resistance to the sin that most easily traps us provides evidence of an upright heart.

Even people who show mercy to others still need mercy from God.

Those faithful to him will discover that he fulfills his promises.

God's word is pure, reliable and sweet.

People who resist him and deliberately live contrary to him will find that he opposes them (Leviticus 26:21–24).

David described a gracious reward that, in general, belongs to those acting from sincere motives.

He spoke comfort to the humble and warning to the proud.

People walking through discouragement and darkness can take courage:

When we praise God for one mercy, we should also remember the countless others that have surrounded us throughout life.

He recognized God's hand in all of them, teaching us to do the same.

From verse 32 onward, Henry sees the gifts by which God equips the spiritual warrior for conflict, following the example of the victorious Leader.

We must seek deliverance through Christ, not through our own strength.

[Ps.18.1-Ps.18.19]
Chapter 18
Chapter Outline
David rejoices in the deliverances God wrought for him. | (1-19) |
He takes the comfort of his integrity, which God had cleared up. | (20-28) |
He gives to God the glory of all his mighty deeds. | (29-50) |
Verses 1-19
The first words, "I will love thee, O Lord, my strength," are the scope and contents of the psalm. Those that truly love God, may triumph in him as their Rock and Refuge, and may with confidence call upon him. It is good for us to observe all the circumstances of a mercy which magnify the power of God and his goodness to us in it. David was a praying man, and God was found a prayer-hearing God. If we pray as he did, we shall speed as he did. God's manifestation of his presence is very fully described, ver. #(7-15). Little appeared of man, but much of God, in these deliverances. It is not possible to apply to the history of the son of Jesse those awful, majestic, and stupendous words which are used through this description of the Divine manifestation. Every part of so solemn a scene of terrors tells us, a greater than David is here. God will not only deliver his people out of their troubles in due time, but he will bear them up under their troubles in the mean time. Can we meditate on ver. 18, without directing one thought to Gethsemane and Calvary? Can we forget that it was in the hour of Christ's deepest calamity, when Judas betrayed, when his friends forsook, when the multitude derided him, and the smiles of his Father's love were withheld, that the powers of darkness prevented him? The sorrows of death surrounded him, in his distress he prayed, [Heb.5.7] He 5:7. God made the earth to shake and tremble, and the rocks to cleave, and brought him out, in his resurrection, because he delighted in him and in his undertaking.
[Ps.18.20-Ps.18.28]
Verses 20-28
Those that forsake the ways of the Lord, depart from their God. But though conscious to ourselves of many a false step, let there not be a wicked departure from our God. David kept his eye upon the rule of God's commands. Constant care to keep from that sin, whatever it be, which most easily besets us, proves that we are upright before God. Those who show mercy to others, even they need mercy. Those who are faithful to God, shall find him all that to them which he has promised to be. The words of the Lord are pure words, very sure to be depended on, and very sweet to be delighted in. Those who resist God, and walk contrary to him, shall find that he will walk contrary to them, [Lev.26.21-Lev.26.24] Le 26:21-24. The gracious recompence of which David spoke, may generally be expected by those who act from right motives. Hence he speaks comfort to the humble, and terror to the proud; "Thou wilt bring down high looks." And he speaks encouragement to himself; "Thou wilt light my candle:" thou wilt revive and comfort my sorrowful spirit; thou wilt guide my way, that I may avoid the snares laid for me. Thou wilt light my candle to work by, and give me an opportunity of serving thee. Let those that walk in darkness, and labour under discouragements, take courage; God himself will be a Light to them.
[Ps.18.29-Ps.18.50]
Verses 29-50
When we praise for one mercy, we must observe the many more, with which we have been compassed all our days. Many things had contributed to David's advancement, and he owns the hand of God in them all, to teach us to do likewise. In verse #(32), and the following verses, are the gifts of God to the spiritual warrior, whereby he is prepared for the contest, after the example of his victorious Leader. Learn that we must seek release being made through Christ, shall be rejected. In David the type, we behold out of trouble through Christ. The prayer put up, without reconciliation Jesus our Redeemer, conflicting with enemies, compassed with sorrows and with floods of ungodly men, enduring not only the pains of death, but the wrath of God for us; yet calling upon the Father with strong cries and tears; rescued from the grave; proceeding to reconcile, or to put under his feet all other enemies, till death, the last enemy, shall be destroyed. We should love the Lord, our Strength, and our Salvation; we should call on him in every trouble, and praise him for every deliverance; we should aim to walk with him in all righteousness and true holiness, keeping from sin. If we belong to him, he conquers and reigns for us, and we shall conquer and reign through him, and partake of the mercy of our anointed King, which is promised to all his seed for evermore. Amen.

Creation declares God's glory (verses 1–6)

The heavens proclaim God's glory, wisdom, power and goodness so clearly that those who ignore him are without excuse.

Their very existence shows that they must have been made by a Creator who is eternal, infinitely wise, powerful and good.

The continuous alternation of day and night displays divine power.

It also reminds us that in Providence, as in nature, God makes light and creates darkness (Isaiah 45:7), placing them alongside each other.

The sun is a picture of Christ, the Sun of Righteousness, the church's Bridegroom and the Light of the World.

Through his gospel he brings divine light and salvation to nations everywhere.

He delights to bless the church he has chosen as his bride.

His course is as tireless as the sun's until the earth is filled with his light and salvation.

We should pray for the day when every nation enjoys the life-giving light of the Savior.

The heavens have no ordinary words or language, yet their voice is heard.

People everywhere can understand this testimony in their own tongue.

Give God the glory for the comfort and benefit received from heavenly lights.

Yet always look beyond them to the Sun of Righteousness.

God's word reveals grace and holiness (verses 7–10)

The Holy Scriptures offer something far more important than day, night, the air we breathe or sunlight.

Fallen human beings need God's word to be restored.

The word translated “law” can also be understood as teaching, embracing everything by which God instructs us in true religion.

The whole is perfect.

It turns the soul away from sin and worldly dependence toward God and holiness.

It shows our sinfulness and misery when we depart from God and the necessity of returning to him.

God's testimony is certain and reliable.

People without education who believe what he says can become wise for salvation.

His word is a trustworthy guide for duty, a living source of comfort and the foundation of lasting hope.

The Lord's statutes are right and bring gladness to the heart.

His commands are pure, holy, just and good.

They reveal our need of the Savior and teach us how to honor his gospel.

The Holy Spirit uses the commandments to enlighten our eyes, showing us sin and misery and guiding us toward duty.

Fear of the Lord, that is, genuine godliness, cleanses our ways and lasts forever.

The ceremonial law has long since ended, but the obligation to fear God has not changed.

His judgments and commands are entirely true and righteous.

Gold serves bodily and temporary interests.

Grace serves the soul and eternity.

God's word received by faith is more precious than gold and sweeter to the soul than honey.

Physical pleasures soon become excessive but never truly satisfy.

The joys of true religion are substantial, lasting and satisfying, without danger of excess.

The word warns and leads us to pray (verses 11–14)

God's word warns the wicked not to continue in evil and warns the righteous not to abandon the good path.

There is a reward not only after keeping God's commands, but in keeping them.

True religion makes our ordinary comforts sweeter and our crosses easier to bear.

It makes life valuable and even death something a believer can welcome.

David wanted forgiveness and cleansing not only for sins he had already discovered and confessed, but also for sins he had forgotten or overlooked.

Everything Scripture teaches us about our guilt should drive us to the throne of grace.

There we should pray.

Our dependence is the same as that of believers who confess that in Jesus Christ alone they have righteousness and strength.

No prayer is acceptable apart from our Redeemer's strength and mediation.

He became our divine Kinsman by taking human nature, so that he could redeem us to God and restore the inheritance we had lost.

May the excellence of God's word deeply affect our hearts, along with the wickedness of sin and the danger sin brings.

His holiness and grace as shown in his word. | (7-10) |
Prayer for the benefit of them. | (11-14) |
Verses 1-6
The heavens so declare the glory of God, and proclaim his wisdom, power, and goodness, that all ungodly men are left without excuse. They speak themselves to be works of God's hands; for they must have a Creator who is eternal, infinitely wise, powerful, and good. The counter-changing of day and night is a great proof of the power of God, and calls us to observe, that, as in the kingdom of nature, so in that of providence, he forms the light, and creates the darkness, [Isa.45.7] Is 45:7, and sets the one against the other. The sun in the firmament is an emblem of the Sun of righteousness, the Bridegroom of the church, and the Light of the world, diffusing Divine light and salvation by his gospel to the nations of the earth. He delights to bless his church, which he has espoused to himself; and his course will be unwearied as that of the sun, till the whole earth is filled with his light and salvation. Let us pray for the time when he shall enlighten, cheer, and make fruitful every nation on earth, with the blessed salvation. They have no speech or language, so some read it, and yet their voice is heard. All people may hear these preachers speak in their own tongue the wonderful works of God. Let us give God the glory of all the comfort and benefit we have by the lights of heaven, still looking above and beyond them to the Sun of righteousness.
[Ps.19.7-Ps.19.10]
Verses 7-10
The Holy Scripture is of much greater benefit to us than day or night, than the air we breathe, or the light of the sun. To recover man out of his fallen state, there is need of the word of God. The word translated "law," may be rendered doctrine, and be understood as meaning all that teaches us true religion. The whole is perfect; its tendency is to convert or turn the soul from sin and the world, to God and holiness. It shows our sinfulness and misery in departing from God, and the necessity of our return to him. This testimony is sure, to be fully depended on: the ignorant and unlearned believing what God saith, become wise unto salvation. It is a sure direction in the way of duty. It is a sure fountain of living comforts, and a sure foundation of lasting hopes. The statues of the Lord are right, just as they should be; and, because they are right, they rejoice the heart. The commandments of the Lord are pure, holy, just, and good. By them we discover our need of a Saviour; and then learn how to adorn his gospel. They are the means which the Holy Spirit uses in enlightening the eyes; they bring us to a sight and sense of our sin and misery, and direct us in the way of duty. The fear of the Lord, that is, true religion and godliness, is clean, it will cleanse our way; and it endureth for ever. The ceremonial law is long since done away, but the law concerning the fear of God is ever the same. The judgments of the Lord, his precepts, are true; they are righteous, and they are so altogether; there is no unrighteousness in any of them. Gold is only for the body, and the concerns of time; but grace is for the soul, and the concerns of eternity. The word of God, received by faith, is more precious than gold; it is sweet to the soul, sweeter than honey. The pleasure of sense soon surfeit, yet never satisfy; but those of religion are substantial and satisfying; there is no danger of excess.
[Ps.19.11-Ps.19.14]
Verses 11-14
God's word warns the wicked not to go on in his wicked way, and warns the righteous not to turn from his good way. There is a reward, not only after keeping, but in keeping God's commandments. Religion makes our comforts sweet, and our crosses easy, life truly valuable, and death itself truly desirable. David not only desired to be pardoned and cleansed from the sins he had discovered and confessed, but from those he had forgotten or overlooked. All discoveries of sin made to us by the law, should drive us to the throne of grace, there to pray. His dependence was the same with that of every Christian who says, Surely in the Lord Jesus have I righteousness and strength. No prayer can be acceptable before God which is not offered in the strength of our Redeemer or Divine Kinsman, through Him who took our nature upon him, that he might redeem us unto God, and restore the long-lost inheritance. May our hearts be much affected with the excellence of the word of God; and much affected with the evil of sin, and the danger we are in of it, and the danger we are in by it.

Original heading

This psalm is a prayer for the kings of Israel, but with relation to Christ.

A prayer for the king in the light of Christ

Even the greatest human beings experience serious trouble.

Neither the crown on a king's head nor grace within the heart makes someone immune to suffering.

Even great people must therefore be people of prayer.

No one should expect to benefit from the prayers of the church or friends while neglecting personal prayer when capable of it.

The psalm asks God to protect the king and preserve his life.

It also asks that the king may continue working for the public good.

We may recognize that God accepts our spiritual sacrifices when his Spirit kindles a holy fire of devotion and love within our souls.

The psalm also asks the Lord to give success to the king's work.

In spiritual warfare, the first step toward victory is trusting only God's mercy and grace.

Those who depend upon themselves will fall.

Believers triumph in God and in the way he has revealed himself to them.

That distinguishes them from people who live as though God did not exist.

Those who praise God's name may also trust God's name.

This was shown when the power and pride of Jewish unbelief and pagan idolatry fell before the preaching and example of humble followers of Jesus.

It remains true in spiritual conflict today.

Believers engage their enemies in Christ's name, Spirit and strength.

It will also be seen at the last day, when the world and its evil prince are brought down.

Then believers will rise through the resurrection of the Lord, stand before him and sing his praise in heaven.

Let us rejoice in the salvation Christ gives.

Raise our banners in the name of the Lord our God.

Through the saving strength of his right hand, we may be confident of victory over every enemy.

Chapter 20
This psalm is a prayer for the kings of Israel, but with relation to Christ.
--Even the greatest of men may be much in trouble. Neither the crown on the king's head, nor the grace in his heart, would make him free from trouble. Even the greatest of men must be much in prayer. Let none expect benefit by the prayers of the church, or their friends, who are capable of praying for themselves, yet neglect it. Pray that God would protect his person, and preserve his life. That God would enable him to go on in his undertakings for the public good. We may know that God accepts our spiritual sacrifices, if by his Spirit he kindles in our souls a holy fire of piety and love to God. Also, that the Lord would crown his enterprises with success. Our first step to victory in spiritual warfare is to trust only in the mercy and grace of God; all who trust in themselves will soon be cast down. Believers triumph in God, and his revelation of himself to them, by which they distinguish themselves from those that live without God in the world. Those who make God and his name their praise, may make God and his name their trust. This was the case when the pride and power of Jewish unbelief, and pagan idolatry, fell before the sermons and lives of the humble believers in Jesus. This is the case in every conflict with our spiritual enemies, when we engage them in the name, the spirit, and the power of Christ; and this will be the case at the last day, when the world, with the prince of it, shall be brought down and fall; but believers, risen-from the dead, through the resurrection of the Lord, shall stand, and sing his praises in heaven. In Christ's salvation let us rejoice; and set up our banners in the name of the Lord our God, assured that by the saving strength of his right hand we shall be conquerors over every enemy.
